title: (Scenario) How would you migrate hundreds of millions of rows without taking the service offline — separate schema compatibility, data movement, application cutover, and cleanup rather than treating the migration as one deployment: introduce the new representation while the old app remains functional, deploy code that operates during transition, backfill historical data in bounded batches with throttling/observability/restartability, verify correctness continuously, and move reads/writes only after confidence is high — and why does a migration that works in staging behave very differently when competing with production traffic?
shortTitle: How do you migrate hundreds of millions of rows without taking the service offline?

s1_definition.profdef: A large online migration is not a single deployment; it is a sequence of independent phases that each preserve a working system: introduce the new schema in a backward-compatible, additive way so the old application keeps functioning; deploy application code that can operate during the transition by writing to both representations; backfill historical data in small, throttled, restartable batches while watching production load; continuously verify that the old and new representations agree; cut reads and then writes over to the new representation only after confidence is high; and finally remove the old representation in a separate cleanup phase. This is the expand-and-contract (also called parallel-change) pattern. It works in production because at no single moment does correctness depend on everything deploying at once, and it respects that a backfill that flew in staging will compete for the same CPU, I/O, locks, and buffer cache as live traffic.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to replace its old paper ledger with a new digital ledger for hundreds of millions of past transactions, but it cannot close for even an hour — Rajesh and Priya must keep transferring money the whole time. So they do it in careful stages. First they install the new digital ledger beside the old paper one without touching the paper one, so the branch keeps working exactly as before. Then every new transaction is written into both the paper ledger and the digital one at the same time. Then, during quiet hours and in small batches, clerks copy old paper records into the digital ledger a little at a time, pausing whenever the branch gets busy so customers are never slowed down. They keep cross-checking that the two ledgers agree. Only once they fully trust the digital ledger do they start reading from it, then writing only to it, and only much later do they throw the old paper ledger away.
s1_definition.oneliner: Treat a huge migration as four separable phases — compatible schema, dual-writing code, throttled restartable backfill with continuous verification, then staged cutover and cleanup — never as one deployment.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A large online migration is not a single deployment; it is a sequence of independent phases that each preserve a working system: introduce the new schema in a backward-compatible, additive way so the old application keeps functioning; deploy application code that can operate during the transition by writing to both representations; backfill historical data in small, throttled, restartable batches while watching production load; continuously verify that the old and new representations agree; cut reads and then writes over to the new representation only after confidence is high; and finally remove the old representation in a separate cleanup phase. This is the expand-and-contract (also called parallel-change) pattern. It works in production because at no single moment does correctness depend on everything deploying at once, and it respects that a backfill that flew in staging will compete for the same CPU, I/O, locks, and buffer cache as live traffic.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to replace its old paper ledger with a new digital ledger for hundreds of millions of past transactions, but it cannot close for even an hour — Rajesh and Priya must keep transferring money the whole time. So they do it in careful stages. First they install the new digital ledger beside the old paper one without touching the paper one, so the branch keeps working exactly as before. Then every new transaction is written into both the paper ledger and the digital one at the same time. Then, during quiet hours and in small batches, clerks copy old paper records into the digital ledger a little at a time, pausing whenever the branch gets busy so customers are never slowed down. They keep cross-checking that the two ledgers agree. Only once they fully trust the digital ledger do they start reading from it, then writing only to it, and only much later do they throw the old paper ledger away.

**One line to remember:** Treat a huge migration as four separable phases — compatible schema, dual-writing code, throttled restartable backfill with continuous verification, then staged cutover and cleanup — never as one deployment.

sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the accounts table stores balances as decimals, and the team wants to store them additionally as integer paise to avoid rounding issues, across hundreds of millions of accounts, with zero downtime.

Problem 1 — a single big UPDATE would lock the table and stall Rajesh's and Priya's live transfers. So the migration must never touch all rows at once.

Problem 2 — new transfers keep happening during the migration, so any plan that backfills a static snapshot would miss changes that occur mid-migration. Dual-writing new changes solves the "moving target" problem; the backfill then only needs to handle historical rows.

Problem 3 — a backfill that worked instantly in staging will fight live traffic in production for locks and I/O, so it must be batched, throttled, restartable, and continuously verified.

The mini-project builds a `MigrationRunner` that performs an additive schema step, enables dual writes, runs a bounded throttled restartable backfill with a checkpoint, continuously verifies old-versus-new agreement, and performs a staged read-then-write cutover. The demo simulates live traffic arriving during the backfill to show dual writes keep new data correct while the backfill handles history, and shows the checkpoint allowing a resume after a simulated crash.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: twenty historical account rows with decimal balances, and a live transfer that arrives in the middle of the migration.

Step 1 — Phase 1, additive schema. A new `balance_minor` column is added as nullable and an index is built concurrently. The old application never references the new column, so Rajesh's and Priya's existing operations are completely unaffected. Nothing locks.

Step 2 — Phase 2, dual write. Rajesh transfers fifty thousand rupees during the migration. The dual-write path sets both his decimal balance to 950,000 and his paise balance to 95,000,000 in the same operation. His new row is already correct without the backfill ever touching it.

Step 3 — Phase 3, backfill begins. The backfill reads rows whose paise balance is still null, in batches of five, converts each decimal to paise, advances the checkpoint, and logs progress. Rajesh's row is skipped because the dual write already filled it.

Step 4 — Phase 3, throttling under load. On alternate checks the production-busy signal is true, so the backfill logs a throttle warning and pauses briefly, yielding resources to live traffic. The checkpoint means that if the process crashed here, it would resume from the last committed batch rather than redo everything.

Step 5 — Phase 4, verification and cutover. The verifier walks every migrated row and confirms the decimal and paise representations agree, finding zero mismatches. With verification clean, the runner reports cutover readiness as true, which is the signal to move reads to the new representation, observe, then move writes, and only much later drop the old column.

```
2026-10-24 18:50:40 [FINE] Dual-write SAV2001 = 950000.00
2026-10-24 18:50:40 [INFO] Backfilled batch up to id=5 total=4
2026-10-24 18:50:40 [WARNING] Production busy — throttling backfill
2026-10-24 18:50:40 [INFO] Backfilled batch up to id=10 total=9
2026-10-24 18:50:40 [WARNING] Production busy — throttling backfill
2026-10-24 18:50:40 [INFO] Backfilled batch up to id=20 total=19
2026-10-24 18:50:40 [INFO] Backfill complete, rows=19
2026-10-24 18:50:40 [INFO] Verification mismatches = 0
2026-10-24 18:50:40 [INFO] Cutover readiness = true (true means move reads to new representation)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  PHASE 1 (schema)      PHASE 2 (dual write)     PHASE 3 (backfill)     PHASE 4 (cutover)
  add balance_minor     live transfer arrives    historical rows        verify agree → 0
  (nullable, CONCURRENT)│                         │ batch of 5           │
  old app unaffected    ▼                         ▼ throttle if busy     ▼
        │          set balance=950000.00     read null-minor rows   reads: old → new
        │          set balance_minor=95000000 convert → paise        then writes: → new
        ▼               │                         │ checkpoint(lastId)   │ (later) DROP old col
  working the whole time, zero downtime, each phase independently reversible until contract
```

```
  ┌────────────┐  REST  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Live Clients│──────→│ Account Service  │  dual-write (old + new)

                     │ Read Replica           │  verification reads here
                     └────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ Backfill Worker              │    │ Verifier (continuous)         │
  │ bounded batches, checkpoint, │    │ sample rows, assert old==new  │
  │ adaptive throttle on p99/lag │    │ mismatch → halt cutover       │
```

```
  ┌─ Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐

  ── Class Diagram ──
  ┌──────────────────┐ uses ┌──────────────┐  uses ┌──────────────┐
  │ MigrationRunner  │─────▶│ Checkpoint   │       │ Verifier     │
  │ + dualWrite()    │      │ + save/lastId│       │ + verify()   │
  │ + backfill()     │─────────────────────────────▶ (reads store)│
  │ + readyForCutover│      └──────────────┘       └──────────────┘
  └────────┬─────────┘
           │ uses
           ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ AccountStore     │  balance (old) + balanceMinor (new)
  └──────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a row's migration state ──
  [OLD ONLY] ──dual-write OR backfill──→ [BOTH IN SYNC] ──verify ok──→ [CUTOVER-READY]
       │                                        │ mismatch
       └────────────────────────────────────── [HALT, INVESTIGATE]

  ── Call Chain (main) ──
  1. ALTER TABLE ADD balance_minor (additive, online)
  2. dualWriteBalance(rajesh, 950000)   → both reps correct
  3. backfill(productionBusy)            → history filled, throttled, checkpointed
  4. verifier.verify()                   → 0 mismatches

```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The core idea is that a migration of hundreds of millions of rows is never a single deployment; it is a sequence of independent phases, each of which leaves a fully working system. I separate four concerns that can fail and be verified independently. First, schema compatibility: I introduce the new representation additively — a new column, table, or index built with online, non-blocking DDL — so the old application, completely unchanged, keeps working and nothing locks against live traffic. Second, transitional code: I deploy application code that dual-writes to both the old and new representations on every change, so from that moment all new data is automatically correct in the new representation while reads still come from the old one, and this step is reversible.

Third, the backfill of historical data, which is where production reality bites. I never run one giant update; I backfill in small bounded batches with a pause between them, with a checkpoint so a crash resumes instead of restarting, with observability on progress and errors, and with an adaptive throttle that backs off the moment live query latency or replication lag rises. The backfill only touches rows the dual-write has not already fixed. Fourth, continuous verification and staged cutover: a verifier samples rows and asserts the old and new representations agree, and only when that is clean do I move reads to the new representation, observe, then move writes exclusively to it, and only in a separate, much later deployment do I drop the old representation in the contract phase. Until that final step, every stage is reversible.

The reason I insist on throttling and batching is that a migration which flew in staging behaves completely differently in production. In staging the backfill owns the database — empty buffer cache, no lock contention, idle disks, no replication lag. In production that same backfill competes with live reads and writes for CPU, disk I/O, the buffer pool, row locks, and replication bandwidth. A backfill that finished in an hour in staging can, in production, cause replica lag, lock timeouts on customer transactions, and I/O saturation. So the throttle has to be driven by live signals, and the whole thing must be pausable and resumable so I can stop it the instant it hurts a customer and continue later.

In my banking work this was exactly how we moved account balances to an integer-paise representation across an enormous table with zero downtime. We added the new column online, dual-wrote every new transfer so moving data never chased a moving target, backfilled history in throttled restartable batches that yielded to live traffic, verified old against new continuously until there were zero mismatches, and only then flipped reads and later writes behind a feature flag, dropping the old column weeks afterward. The principle I take into interviews is that the goal is not to perform the migration quickly; it is to ensure there is never a single moment where correctness depends on everything happening at once, because that single moment is exactly where downtime and data loss live.
